topic: Everest death zone: low oxygen, no acclimatization, thick blood, brain swelling, record-low blood oxygen
hook: What the death zone does to your body
caption:
Above 8,000 meters, the human body starts dying slowly. In 2007, doctors drew blood from climbers near Everest's summit. Their oxygen levels were among the lowest ever measured in living people.

The body can't adapt up there. Blood thickens, fluid can leak into the brain, and climbers lose muscle by the day. Most summit pushes are a race against the clock. Save this for the next time someone calls Everest 'just a long hike.'

Follow for one fact your brain won't believe, every day. Would you ever try to climb Everest?

Above 8,000 meters, the human body starts dying slowly. In 2007, doctors drew blood from climbers near Everest's summit. Their oxygen levels were among the lowest ever measured in living people.

The body can't adapt up there. Blood thickens, fluid can leak into the brain, and climbers lose muscle by the day. Most summit pushes are a race against the clock. Save this for the next time someone calls Everest 'just a long hike.'

Follow for one fact your brain won't believe, every day. Would you ever try to climb Everest?

Cover: What the death zone does to your body
📷 Goutam1962 (CC BY-SA 4.0) via wikimedia

1/5 Above 8,000 meters (8000m)
Climbers call it the death zone. Air pressure is about a third of sea level, so each breath brings far less oxygen.
📷 Debasish biswas kolkata
Derivative work MagentaGreen (CC BY-SA 4.0) via wikimedia

2/5 Your body can't adapt
Up there, nobody can fully acclimatize. The body slowly breaks down, losing weight and muscle the longer it stays.
📷 Paxson Woelber (CC BY 2.0) via wikimedia

3/5 Blood turns thick
The body makes extra red blood cells to carry oxygen. Thicker blood raises the risk of clots and strokes.
📷 Arek Socha (CC0) via wikimedia

4/5 Fluid floods the brain (Hours)
Low oxygen can make vessels leak. Fluid in the brain or lungs can kill within hours unless climbers descend.
🎨 AI-generated image

5/5 Blood oxygen hits bottom (-75%)
Blood samples taken near Everest's summit showed oxygen levels about 75% below normal, among the lowest ever recorded in humans.
📷 Vyacheslav Argenberg (CC BY 4.0) via wikimedia
